duckrev: rerun only the stages whose DuckDB tables really changed

The problem it solves

A DVC pipeline decides what to rerun by hashing files. That works until all stages read one DuckDB database that a stage modifies during the run: DVC cannot look inside a .duckdb file. Track the whole file and every change reruns everything. Track nothing and a stage never learns that its input changed. Caching every table as a separate file per version would work, but with large data I do not want a copy of each step in each version. I only want the most recent state.

The general idea

Give every table and view a rev: a tiny text file that fingerprints it. DVC tracks the rev files, not the database. A downstream stage depends on the rev of exactly what it reads, so a change travels only as far as it is visible. The rev has three levels, and the helper computes only the cheap ones unless asked:

  • catalog: a hash of the CREATE statement (and the estimated size for a table). It reads no data.
  • rows: the exact row count. It needs a scan.
  • row_hash: the sum of the hash of every row, so the row order does not matter. It needs a scan.

The pipeline has a clean stage that always runs first. It compares each rev file with the live database and deletes the ones that no longer match. For DVC a missing output means the stage that writes it is stale, so build runs again and writes new revs. If a table was edited by hand, the revs are rebuilt too, and when the data ends up identical, nothing downstream reruns.

raw/orders.csv -> clean -> build -> daily -> summary
                                \-> export

Examples

The helper is one small module. A rev is built from the catalog and, when scan_rows is on, from a hash over the rows:

def scan_table(con, obj):
    schema, name = split(obj)
    count, total = con.execute(
        f'SELECT count(*), coalesce(sum(hash(t)::HUGEINT), 0) FROM "{schema}"."{name}" t'
    ).fetchone()
    return count, str(total)

The pipeline reads like any other DVC pipeline. build writes the revs, and each downstream depends on one rev only:

stages:
  clean:
    cmd: uv run duckrev clean -d wh.duckdb -r main.sales main.v_sales_by_day
    always_changed: true
    outs:
      - revs/.cleaned: {cache: false}
  build:
    cmd: uv run duckrev -d wh.duckdb -c sql/build.sql -r main.sales main.v_sales_by_day
    deps: [sql/build.sql, raw/orders.csv, revs/.cleaned]
    outs:
      - revs/wh__main__sales.rev: {cache: false}
      - revs/wh__main__v_sales_by_day.rev: {cache: false}
  daily:
    cmd: uv run python -m utils.downstream daily
    deps: [revs/wh__main__v_sales_by_day.rev]
    outs: [out/daily.csv]
  export:
    cmd: uv run python -m utils.downstream export
    deps: [revs/wh__main__sales.rev]
    outs: [out/sales.parquet]

Now the raw data changes. Upstream relabels web to online in a column that the daily view never reads:

sed -i '' 's/,web,/,online,/' raw/orders.csv
dvc repro
# Running stage 'clean'
# Running stage 'build'
# Stage 'daily' didn't change, skipping
# Running stage 'export'
# Stage 'summary' didn't change, skipping

The sales table changed, so build and export run. The view v_sales_by_day gets the same rev as before, so daily and summary are skipped. New rows rerun everything. A changed view definition reruns the view's consumers and leaves export alone. A hand edit like UPDATE sales SET amount = 0 is noticed by clean and repaired by build.

Tips from my setup

  • Every rev output says cache: false. Otherwise DVC's run cache can answer "same inputs as an earlier run" by restoring old revs instead of running build. A hand edit would stay in the database while the revs claim it is clean. The helper stops the pipeline if a rev output lacks the flag. Commit the rev files: they are tiny and their history shows in git diffs.
  • Two stages must not change the same table. A rev belongs to one stage, and DVC does not allow two stages to share an output. If two stages wrote the same table, neither could tell its own change from the other's.
  • scan_rows is a switch in params.yaml. On, the check also hashes every row and catches changes that keep the definition. Off, it reads the catalog only, which is free on large tables.
  • No new files. The only artifacts are the revs and the stage outputs. The database stays one file that is edited in place, so an ML pipeline with large data keeps just the most recent version, not a cached copy of each step in each version.
  • The change in the raw data is recorded. The rev files change in git, so the history shows which table moved and when.
